content: Arogyini | Constitutional Women's Rights RAG Reference | English Page 1 THE CONSTITUTION OF INDIA Constitutional Rights and Protections Relevant to Women English-language thematic extraction for the Arogyini RAG knowledge base Purpose. This guide identifies constitutional provisions that are directly or materially relevant to women's equality, dignity, safety, participation, education, work, health, political representation and access to justice. It is a structured study aid, not a substitute for the full Constitution, current legislation or legal advice. Important method note. The explanations below are concise paraphrases, not quotations of the constitutional text. The wording of the Constitution should be retrieved from the official source when an exact quotation is needed. The guide is in English only

. The wording of the Constitution should be retrieved from the official source when an exact quotation is needed. The guide is in English only. Coverage at a glance Theme Main constitutional provisions Equality and non-discrimination Preamble; Articles 14, 15, 16 Dignity, liberty, privacy and bodily autonomy Articles 19, 21, 21A; judicial interpretation Protection from trafficking and exploitation Articles 23 and 24 Work, equal pay and maternity relief Articles 39, 39A, 41, 42 and 43 Education, nutrition and social welfare Articles 21A, 45, 46 and 47 Gender equality as a civic duty Article 51A(e) Women's political participation Articles 243D, 243T, 325, 326, 330A, 332A and 334A Arogyini | Constitutional Women's Rights RAG Reference | English Page 2 1. Foundational constitutional values and enforceable rights Preamble. The Preamble commits India to justice (social, economic and political), liberty, equality of status and opportunity, and individual dignity. It is not ordinarily a standalone source of an independently enforceable claim, but it guides constitutional interpretation

. It is not ordinarily a standalone source of an independently enforceable claim, but it guides constitutional interpretation. Article 14: Equality before law and equal protection of the laws Core meaning: The State must treat persons equally before the law and provide equal protection of the laws within India. Relevance to women's rights: A foundational basis for challenging arbitrary State action and unequal treatment affecting women. It supports substantive equality analysis, not merely identical treatment in every circumstance. RAG keywords: equality before law; equal protection; arbitrariness; gender equality; State discrimination Legal character: Fundamental Right; enforceable subject to constitutional doctrine. Article 15(1): Prohibition of discrimination on specified grounds Core meaning: The State must not discriminate against a citizen only on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth, or any of them. Relevance to women's rights: Expressly prohibits State discrimination on the ground of sex. It is central to challenges involving unequal access to public services, opportunities or benefits

. Relevance to women's rights: Expressly prohibits State discrimination on the ground of sex. It is central to challenges involving unequal access to public services, opportunities or benefits. RAG keywords: sex discrimination; State action; discrimination against women; equal access Article 15(3): Special provisions for women and children Core meaning: Article 15 does not prevent the State from making special provisions for women and children. Relevance to women's rights: Constitutional basis for protective and affirmative measures for women, including targeted welfare, support, representation or safeguards. A measure should still be assessed for its purpose and constitutional validity. RAG keywords: special provisions for women; affirmative action; protective discrimination; women and children Article 15(4) and 15(5): Special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes and specified groups Core meaning: These clauses enable specified special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, including in educational settings as constitutionally defined

. Relevance to women's rights: May be relevant to women who also belong to constitutionally recognised disadvantaged groups. These clauses are not women-specific provisions. RAG keywords: intersectionality; backward classes; SC; ST; educational admission; social disadvantage Article 16: Equality of opportunity in public employment Core meaning: Citizens must have equality of opportunity in matters relating to employment or appointment to an office under the State, subject to the article's permitted exceptions and reservation framework. Relevance to women's rights: Relevant to sex-based exclusion, unequal recruitment conditions and discrimination in public employment. Article 16(2) expressly includes sex among prohibited grounds. RAG keywords: public employment; equal opportunity; sex discrimination; recruitment; promotion Article 19: Freedoms of citizens Core meaning: Protects specified freedoms, including speech and expression, peaceful assembly, association, movement, residence and profession or occupation, subject to constitutionally permitted reasonable restrictions

. Relevance to women's rights: Supports women's ability to speak, organise, protest, travel, reside and pursue livelihoods. Restrictions must satisfy the constitutional standards applicable to the particular freedom. RAG keywords: freedom of speech; association; movement; residence; occupation; women's participation Arogyini | Constitutional Women's Rights RAG Reference | English Page 3 Article 21: Protection of life and personal liberty Core meaning: No person may be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. Judicial interpretation has given this protection broad content. Relevance to women's rights: A key constitutional foundation for dignity, privacy, bodily integrity, decisional autonomy, reproductive choice and protection of personal liberty. Specific claims depend on facts, precedent and applicable law. RAG keywords: life; personal liberty; dignity; privacy; bodily autonomy; reproductive choice; consent; safety Article 21A: Right to education Core meaning: The State must provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of six to fourteen years in the manner determined by law

. Relevance to women's rights: Important for girls' access to elementary education and the State's constitutional education obligation. Detailed implementation is governed by legislation and policy. RAG keywords: girls' education; free compulsory education; children aged 6 to 14 Article 23: Prohibition of trafficking and forced labour Core meaning: Prohibits trafficking in human beings, begar and other similar forms of forced labour. Contravention is punishable in accordance with law. Relevance to women's rights: Directly relevant to trafficking of women and girls, forced labour, coercive exploitation and practices that deprive people of meaningful freedom. RAG keywords: human trafficking; forced labour; begar; exploitation; women and girls Article 24: Prohibition of child employment in specified work Core meaning: Prohibits employment of children below fourteen years in factories, mines or other hazardous employment. Relevance to women's rights: Relevant to the protection of girls from hazardous child labour. It is a child-protection provision, not a women-only provision

. Relevance to women's rights: Relevant to the protection of girls from hazardous child labour. It is a child-protection provision, not a women-only provision. RAG keywords: child labour; girls; hazardous employment; under fourteen Arogyini | Constitutional Women's Rights RAG Reference | English Page 4 2. Directive Principles: work, welfare, health and justice Directive Principles of State Policy guide governance and law-making. Under Article 37 they are not enforceable by a court in the same way as Fundamental Rights, but they are declared fundamental in the governance of the country and inform interpretation and public policy. Article 38: Social order for the promotion of welfare Core meaning: The State should promote a social order informed by social, economic and political justice and minimise inequalities. Relevance to women's rights: Provides a broad policy foundation for addressing structural inequalities that disproportionately affect women, including unequal access to resources and opportunities. RAG keywords: social justice; welfare; inequality; gender inequality; social order Legal character: Directive Principle; not independently enforceable

. RAG keywords: social justice; welfare; inequality; gender inequality; social order Legal character: Directive Principle; not independently enforceable. Article 39(a): Adequate means of livelihood Core meaning: The State should direct policy towards ensuring that men and women equally have the right to an adequate means of livelihood. Relevance to women's rights: Explicitly recognises livelihood for both women and men. Relevant to women's economic security, access to work and livelihood programmes. RAG keywords: adequate livelihood; women and men; economic security; employment Article 39(d): Equal pay for equal work Core meaning: The State should direct policy towards equal pay for equal work for both men and women. Relevance to women's rights: An express constitutional policy commitment against sex-based wage inequality. Enforceable outcomes are shaped by legislation and judicial interpretation

. Relevance to women's rights: An express constitutional policy commitment against sex-based wage inequality. Enforceable outcomes are shaped by legislation and judicial interpretation. RAG keywords: equal pay; equal remuneration; wage discrimination; men and women Article 39(e): Protection of workers' health and strength Core meaning: The State should ensure that the health and strength of workers, men and women, and the tender age of children are not abused, and that economic necessity does not force people into work unsuited to their age or strength. Relevance to women's rights: Relevant to unsafe working conditions, exploitation of women workers and protection from work that harms health or dignity. RAG keywords: women workers; occupational health; exploitation; unsafe work Article 39(f): Healthy development and protection of children Core meaning: Children should have opportunities and facilities to develop in a healthy manner and in conditions of freedom and dignity, with protection against exploitation and abandonment. Relevance to women's rights: Relevant to girls' development, safety and protection from exploitation, including where gender-based harms affect children

. Relevance to women's rights: Relevant to girls' development, safety and protection from exploitation, including where gender-based harms affect children. RAG keywords: girl child; child development; dignity; exploitation; protection Article 39A: Equal justice and free legal aid Core meaning: The State should ensure that the legal system promotes justice on the basis of equal opportunity and provide free legal aid through suitable legislation, schemes or other means. Relevance to women's rights: Important for women who face financial, social or other barriers to legal representation and access to justice. Eligibility and delivery are governed by legal aid laws and rules. RAG keywords: free legal aid; access to justice; equal opportunity; legal representation Arogyini | Constitutional Women's Rights RAG Reference | English Page 5 Article 41: Right to work, education and public assistance in specified cases Core meaning: Within its economic capacity and development, the State should make effective provision for work, education and public assistance in cases such as unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement, and other cases of undeserved want

. Relevance to women's rights: Relevant to social security and public assistance for women facing vulnerability, subject to the State's capacity and applicable schemes. RAG keywords: public assistance; social security; sickness; unemployment; women in need Article 42: Just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief Core meaning: The State should make provision for just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief. Relevance to women's rights: The clearest Directive Principle specifically referring to maternity relief. It informs maternity-benefit legislation, workplace protections and policies supporting safe and humane work. RAG keywords: maternity relief; maternity benefit; humane working conditions; pregnant workers Article 43: Living wage and decent standard of life Core meaning: The State should endeavour to secure work, a living wage, conditions ensuring a decent standard of life, leisure and social and cultural opportunities for workers. Relevance to women's rights: Relevant to fair work and economic dignity for women workers, including those in informal or low-paid sectors, as a policy principle

. Relevance to women's rights: Relevant to fair work and economic dignity for women workers, including those in informal or low-paid sectors, as a policy principle. RAG keywords: living wage; decent standard of life; women workers; labour welfare Article 45: Early childhood care and education Core meaning: The State should endeavour to provide early childhood care and education for all children until they complete six years of age. Relevance to women's rights: Relevant to early childhood services and care infrastructure, which can support children's development and reduce care burdens that often affect women's participation in education and work. RAG keywords: early childhood care; preschool; child care; care infrastructure Article 46: Promotion of educational and economic interests of weaker sections Core meaning: The State should promote with special care the educational and economic interests of weaker sections, particularly Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, and protect them from social injustice and exploitation. Relevance to women's rights: Relevant to women who experience overlapping disadvantage based on caste, tribe, education or economic status

. Relevance to women's rights: Relevant to women who experience overlapping disadvantage based on caste, tribe, education or economic status. It is not a women-specific clause. RAG keywords: weaker sections; SC women; ST women; education; economic interests; exploitation Article 47: Nutrition, standard of living and public health Core meaning: The State should regard raising nutrition levels, standards of living and improving public health as among its primary duties. Relevance to women's rights: Supports public-health policy relevant to women's nutrition, maternal health and access to health services. Specific entitlements arise through legislation, schemes and other law. RAG keywords: public health; nutrition; maternal health; standard of living Arogyini | Constitutional Women's Rights RAG Reference | English Page 6 3. Fundamental Duties and democratic participation Article 51A(e): Duty to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women Core meaning: It is the duty of every citizen to promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood and to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women

. Relevance to women's rights: The Constitution expressly identifies practices derogatory to women's dignity as something citizens should renounce. It is a Fundamental Duty, not by itself a standalone criminal offence or directly enforceable individual claim. RAG keywords: dignity of women; harmful practices; gender respect; citizen duty; equality Article 51A(k): Duty of parent or guardian regarding education Core meaning: A parent or guardian has a duty to provide opportunities for education to a child or ward between six and fourteen years of age. Relevance to women's rights: Relevant to social responsibility for girls' education. Read alongside Article 21A and education legislation. RAG keywords: girls' education; parent duty; guardian; school attendance Local self-government: reservation for women Article 243D(3): Reservation of seats for women in Panchayats Core meaning: Not less than one-third of the total seats to be filled by direct election in every Panchayat are to be reserved for women, including the number of seats reserved for women belonging to the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes

. Relevance to women's rights: Creates a constitutional minimum for women's representation in Panchayats. State laws may provide for a higher proportion. RAG keywords: Panchayat; one-third reservation; women representatives; local government Article 243D(4): Reservation of chairperson offices in Panchayats Core meaning: Not less than one-third of the total number of offices of chairpersons in Panchayats at each level are to be reserved for women, in the manner provided by State law. Relevance to women's rights: Supports women's leadership in rural local government. RAG keywords: Panchayat chairperson; women leadership; local government reservation Article 243T(3): Reservation of seats for women in Municipalities Core meaning: Not less than one-third of the total seats to be filled by direct election in every Municipality are to be reserved for women, including seats within the SC/ST reservation. Relevance to women's rights: Constitutional minimum for women's representation in urban local bodies. State law determines implementation details

. Relevance to women's rights: Constitutional minimum for women's representation in urban local bodies. State law determines implementation details. RAG keywords: Municipality; urban local government; women reservation; elected seats Article 243T(4): Reservation of chairperson offices in Municipalities Core meaning: The manner of reservation of offices of chairpersons in Municipalities is to be provided by State law. Relevance to women's rights: Enables State-level arrangements for women's representation in municipal leadership; the exact reservation design depends on the relevant State law. RAG keywords: municipal chairperson; women leadership; State law Arogyini | Constitutional Women's Rights RAG Reference | English Page 7 4. Elections and representation in Parliament and State Assemblies Article 325: One general electoral roll; no exclusion on grounds including sex Core meaning: No person is to be ineligible for inclusion in a special electoral roll, or claim inclusion in a general electoral roll, on grounds only of religion, race, caste or sex

. Relevance to women's rights: Protects women's equal inclusion in electoral rolls and rejects sex-based exclusion from voter registration. RAG keywords: voter registration; electoral roll; sex discrimination; voting rights Article 326: Elections on the basis of adult suffrage Core meaning: Elections to the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies are based on adult suffrage, subject to constitutional and statutory qualifications. Relevance to women's rights: Women who meet the applicable qualifications have equal voting rights. This provision supports equal political citizenship. RAG keywords: adult suffrage; women voters; voting rights; elections 106th Constitutional Amendment: women's reservation in legislatures Article 330A: Reservation of seats for women in the House of the People Core meaning: Provides for reservation of seats for women in the Lok Sabha, including reservation within the seats reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, subject to the constitutional design. Relevance to women's rights: Creates the constitutional framework for one-third reservation of seats for women in the Lok Sabha. Its commencement and operation are linked to Article 334A

. Relevance to women's rights: Creates the constitutional framework for one-third reservation of seats for women in the Lok Sabha. Its commencement and operation are linked to Article 334A. RAG keywords: Lok Sabha; women reservation; 106th Amendment; one-third seats Article 332A: Reservation of seats for women in State Legislative Assemblies Core meaning: Provides for reservation of seats for women in State Legislative Assemblies, including within the SC/ST-reserved seats, subject to the constitutional design. Relevance to women's rights: Creates the constitutional framework for one-third reservation of seats for women in State Assemblies, with operation linked to Article 334A. RAG keywords: State Assembly; women reservation; legislative representation; 106th Amendment Article 334A: When legislative reservation takes effect and its duration Core meaning: Provides that the reservation under Articles 330A and 332A takes effect after the relevant figures of the first census taken after commencement of the 106th Amendment have been published and a delimitation exercise is undertaken for this purpose. It also addresses the duration and rotation framework

. It also addresses the duration and rotation framework. Relevance to women's rights: Essential for accurate answers about when women's reservation in Parliament and State Assemblies becomes operational. Do not tell users that the one-third reservation is already in operation without checking the latest commencement, census and delimitation position. RAG keywords: implementation; commencement; census; delimitation; rotation; 106th Amendment Arogyini | Constitutional Women's Rights RAG Reference | English Page 8 5. Important constitutional interpretation through Supreme Court decisions These decisions are not constitutional articles. They are judicial authorities that help explain how constitutional rights and principles have been applied. For a production RAG corpus, ingest the full judgments from an authoritative court source and retain case name, court, date, citation and paragraph numbers. Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) The Supreme Court framed workplace sexual-harassment guidelines in the absence of specific legislation, relying on equality, non-discrimination, life and dignity guarantees and relevant international principles

. The guidelines operated until legislation was enacted. RAG tags: Articles 14, 15, 19(1)(g), 21; workplace sexual harassment; safe working environment. Suchita Srivastava v. Chandigarh Administration (2009) Recognised reproductive choice as an aspect of personal liberty under Article 21, including the importance of a woman's decisional autonomy. RAG tags: Article 21; reproductive autonomy; bodily integrity; consent. National Legal Services Authority v. Union of India (2014) Recognised constitutional protections for gender identity and dignity, including the rights of transgender persons. It is relevant to an inclusive understanding of gender equality, though not limited to women. RAG tags: Articles 14, 15, 16, 19, 21; gender identity; dignity; transgender rights. Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017) The Supreme Court invalidated instant triple talaq by a majority, with differing opinions and reasoning among the judges. The decision is relevant to equality, dignity and personal-law debates; describe the holding carefully rather than reducing it to a single constitutional proposition. RAG tags: marriage; personal law; equality; dignity; instant triple talaq. Independent Thought v

. RAG tags: marriage; personal law; equality; dignity; instant triple talaq. Independent Thought v. Union of India (2017) Read the marital-rape exception in the criminal law narrowly in relation to a wife below eighteen years, harmonising the law with the protection of children. It is relevant to bodily integrity and child protection. RAG tags: child marriage; sexual violence; bodily integrity; Article 21; girls below 18. Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018) Struck down the adultery offence in the former Indian Penal Code as unconstitutional, rejecting a framework that treated women as subordinate or as the property of their husbands. RAG tags: Articles 14, 15, 21; autonomy; equality in marriage; dignity. Arogyini | Constitutional Women's Rights RAG Reference | English Page 9 6

How to use this guide in a women-rights RAG system Recommended document metadata Field Suggested value / rule document_title Constitution of India - Women's Rights Extract jurisdiction India document_type Constitutional provision guide / secondary study aid language English source_authority Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice, Government of India source_version Use the latest official Constitution edition and record its 'as on' date provision_id Article number and clause, e.g. Article 15(3) topic Equality, dignity, employment, maternity, political representation, etc. legal_character Fundamental Right / Directive Principle / Fundamental Duty / electoral provision text_type Paraphrase; not verbatim constitutional text effective_status Verify amendment, commencement and current legal position before answering Recommended chunking strategy 1. Create one primary chunk per article clause, not one chunk for the entire chapter. 2

. Create one primary chunk per article clause, not one chunk for the entire chapter. 2. Keep the article number, heading, legal character and topic tags inside every chunk so retrieved passages remain self-identifying. 3. Store the exact official constitutional text separately from this paraphrase. Use the exact text as the primary evidence and this guide as explanatory metadata. 4. For multi-clause articles such as Article 15, create separate chunks for 15(1), 15(3), 15(4) and 15(5), while linking them to the parent Article 15. 5. For Articles 330A, 332A and 334A, retrieve the commencement and delimitation condition together. This prevents misleading claims about the immediate implementation of legislative reservation. 6. Attach judgment paragraphs as separate authority chunks. Do not merge judicial interpretation into the constitutional text. 7. When answering a user, distinguish a constitutional right, a Directive Principle, a Fundamental Duty and a statutory remedy. Answering safeguards for the chatbot  Do not say every Directive Principle is directly enforceable in court. Article 37 distinguishes Directive Principles from enforceable Fundamental Rights

. Answering safeguards for the chatbot  Do not say every Directive Principle is directly enforceable in court. Article 37 distinguishes Directive Principles from enforceable Fundamental Rights.  Do not describe Article 51A(e) as creating a standalone criminal offence. It is a Fundamental Duty.  Do not imply that Article 15(3) automatically validates every measure labelled as protective. Explain the measure and its legal context.  Do not state that all women-specific protections come from the Constitution. Many concrete remedies arise under statutes, rules and schemes.  Do not state that the one-third reservation in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies is already operational without verifying the latest census, delimitation and commencement status under Article 334A.  When a question concerns a specific remedy, retrieve the relevant current statute as well as the constitutional principle. Primary sources and verification Primary constitutional source: Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice, Government of India

. Primary sources and verification Primary constitutional source: Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice, Government of India. Use the latest English text available through the official Constitution documents page. The official document listing is maintained at: https://www.legislative.gov.in/documents Official Constitution PDF (Legislative Department, 2025 publication) Amendment source: The Constitution (One Hundred and Sixth Amendment) Act, 2023 is the source of Articles 330A, 332A and 334A. Confirm the latest official amendment text and commencement status before operational use. Verification date of this guide: 1 November 2026. Before deployment, re-check the latest official Constitution text, amendments, commencement notifications and relevant judgments. Scope and limitations This guide is a curated thematic extraction, not an exhaustive list of every constitutional provision that could affect women. Provisions concerning citizenship, religious and cultural rights, minority institutions, emergency powers, federal relations, public health and State-specific arrangements may also become relevant depending on the user's facts

. The Constitution applies to persons and citizens in different ways; for example, Articles 14 and 21 protect persons, while Articles 15, 16 and 19 are framed in terms of citizens. The distinction matters and should be preserved in answers. This document is educational material for knowledge-base preparation. It is not legal advice. For individual cases, consult a qualified lawyer or an appropriate legal services authority.
